item.title: New Hope for When the Fear of Failure Gets You Down
item.description:
Therapy

New Hope for When the Fear of Failure Gets You Down

A specific imagery-based therapy may bring relief.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Many therapy clients become stuck due to their fear of failure.
  • Imagery Rescripting (ImRs) is aims to change the way that memories play out in the mind.
  • Research found that this approach produced reductions in sadness, fear of failure, and guilt.

Over my many years of clinical practice within anxiety disorders, I’ve worked with innumerable clients who are stuck in the rut of fear of failure. There are many potential causes of this, from rigidly perfectionistic attitudes to an identity that is based too largely upon achievement. Not uncommonly, it is painful memories from childhood that can be a driving factor in developing this fear. Emotional abuse, overly harsh criticism, and neglect can have ripple effects that impact self-worth even decades later.

How did your parents or other caregivers respond to your mistakes when you were a child? Did they berate you, leaving you scared of their potential outbursts to the point of denying you a voice to defend yourself? Learning that making mistakes is something to fear at all costs can become a vicious cycle throughout development, where you become scared to take new risks — which denies you practice in handling mistakes, which makes mistakes even less scary, perpetuating the cycle. And this pattern can continue into adulthood, especially with regard to how you feel about “messing up." Does making mistakes make you feel less worthy?

If so, exciting new research brings hope about treatment.

A recent study from the Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at SWPS University in Warsaw suggests that a specialized imagery-based psychotherapy can help reduce the pain of these childhood memories.

The study had 180 adult participants, between the ages of 18 and 35, who all reported experiencing the fear of failure, took part in two weeks of therapy sessions that targeted childhood memories of harsh criticism. In one group, participants were supported in using the Imagery Exposure (IE) technique, where they were asked simply to recall situations that had triggered fear or anxiety. This served as a control group, where memories were evoked, but not changed.

In the second group, participants were instructed to use Imagery Rescripting (ImRs), which is a more active technique designed to change the way that memories play out in your mind. Once participants recalled the upsetting experience, they then imagined someone supportive defending them in the aftermath, directly confronting the overly critical person, and offering support to the participant's childhood self.

Finally, the third group used this ImRs approach but with a 10-minute delay between recalling the memory and imagining the support.

Various assessments were given after the interventions and then again three and six months later, and strikingly, all of the approaches produced reductions in sadness, fear of failure, and guilt. This was even shown physiologically, with less bodily reactivity to the memories, even at three and six months, suggesting that a general exposure effect of recalling the distressing memories in a safe environment was beneficial.

The most beneficial effects, however, came from the Imagery Rescripting effect without delay. The researchers surmise that part of why this worked particularly well is that it defied expectations: the element of surprise is important. A participant might expect the memory to play out with their childhood self having been left undefended and unsupported, and instead, the memory is jostled into a new outcome that defies their expectations, making it more likely that new cognitive pathways developed — and stuck.

So, if there is a particularly painful memory from childhood that continues to eat away at you, perhaps you can try, gently, self-help version of this. As it comes to mind, rewrite the script and imagine a supportive, helpful crusader coming to your defense. It just might make a difference!

item.title: What If One Gene Could Erase Your Personality?
item.description:
Personality

What If One Gene Could Erase Your Personality?

An interview with the author of "The Vanishing Family."

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • A new book follows a family with an inherited form of FTD, a type of early-onset dementia.
  • The book explores how family members confront the possibility of losing their personalities.
  • Like many rare diseases, FTD has been largely overlooked by drug companies.

Imagine a genetic disease with the following characteristics. If you're born into a family that has it, there's a 50-50 chance you'll have the following life course. In your 40s, you'll start acting strangely, only you won't recognize that it's strange; everyone else will. You might lose your inhibitions, say mean things, and stop caring for yourself or your home. In time, you may begin isolating yourself, spending your days watching TV and chain-smoking. Eventually, you may lose the ability to speak and become a shell of yourself, needing help with the most basic functions.

This disease has a name: an inherited form of frontotemporal dementia, or FTD.

Source: Penguin Random House

Robert Kolker, bestselling author of Hidden Valley Road, tells the story of one family with this disease in his new book, The Vanishing Family: Love, Fate, and the Quest to End Dementia. It's a heartbreaking journey into a poorly understood illness that slowly chips away at our very selves.

I interviewed Robert Kolker about how he came to this family, why some members chose not to learn their genetic fate, and what FTD reveals about the self.

JG: Can you recount how you came across this family?

RK: This family found me. They had read Hidden Valley Road, and one member of the family contacted me and said, "We have a rare disease, and we have nine children in our family." I had just spent several years researching schizophrenia, which, as you know, has no single known cause, genetic or otherwise. And this family was telling me that they had an incurable disease, but that they knew exactly what the cause was: a genetic cause, a mutation, one gene. And I said, "Aren't we in the era of genetic editing? Couldn't CRISPR or some other tool wipe out this problem by lunch tomorrow?" And she said, "That's what we would like to know."

Unlike Alzheimer's, which affects cognition and memory, their illness hits personality first. The people they care most about, they suddenly don't seem to care much about. And it's heartbreaking, of course, but it also raises the question: if all it takes to change your personality is one gene that goes awry, what is a personality? Why are we the people we are?

And really, the question that I found most relatable: what is it about any of us that is real and lasting? I know, personally, I'm going to be a very different person at age 80 than I was at age 16. But this kind of drastic change raises the question of what it is about us that makes us us to begin with.

That really got me. It took my breath away, that question, because in short order I found a lot of researchers who are drawn to FTD for that same reason. They think FTD is the place where psychiatry and neurobiology bump up against one another and overlap a little bit, and it's almost a key to understanding the roots of the self.

JG: You talk about family members who decided not to get tested, and I really found myself judging that. I dabble in medical ethics, and it seemed to me that if I knew there was a 50-50 chance I was going to be completely dependent on my family, I'd have an obligation to prepare as best I could. How did the ones who declined testing justify that to themselves?

RK: When I was starting to work on this, I thought that if I were in this position, I would want all the facts as soon as possible. I thought, "I'm a reporter. I want to know all the information. I want to know what I'm dealing with." After a while, what started out seeming like rationalization started to feel like authentic, visceral reactions to what was going on in their lives.

There's one person who had spent her whole childhood watching her mother vanish—disappear before her eyes. And by the time she found out that she could take this test, she was already married, a mother with kids who were becoming teenagers. So it was like three different nightmares all happening at once: she might have it, the kids might have it, and they might pass it down. So she suffers in silence for 10 years, and it takes a toll, until finally she's ready to learn the truth.

The one woman who went ahead and had kids, even though she knew she was positive, had tried selective embryo transfer, and it hadn't worked. When she got pregnant, she decided, "Who's to say what anyone's future holds?" From our point of view, maybe she's rationalizing, but she was choosing radical optimism. She was saying, "Who's to say there won't be a cure? Who is anyone to tell me that I'm unethical to have a child based on my genetic makeup? Why is that wrong?"

JG: I was thinking about how mental illness often comes in two kinds. One is just distressing to have, like depression. And others are not so much distressing for the person who has it, but really unpleasant for other people, like antisocial personality disorder. I know that FTD is not a mental illness, but as I was reading your book, I kept thinking it seemed closer to the second kind—that it didn't seem inherently awful to have, but obviously awful for the caretakers and families watching this person, or losing this person.

RK: You're right that in most cases the people are not suffering overtly and do not believe that they're sick. They have anosognosia. The thing that's most fascinating to me is that as soon as they had a real diagnosis, several members of this family were talking to each other about how they would want to end their lives if they learned that they were starting to change. And none of them have. One by one, many of them have changed, and none of them have opted to harm themselves. So I think you dread it in advance, but once you have it, it's really more of a tragedy for the people around you.

And then you become enmeshed with this new person and even love them. You see a drastic version of this in The Vanishing Family with Sue caring for Christy for 30 years. This woman could not be more different because of her illness, and her sister loves her anyway and cares for her every day.

JG: You point out that FTD shares the fate of a lot of rare diseases. What would really move the needle treatment-wise?

RK: It's an exciting moment right now, because there are a lot of researchers and pharmaceutical companies who are interested in the tau protein and how it plays out in lots of dementias, including Alzheimer's. This family and a lot of FTD families have a tau issue. So they could get a trickle-down effect from all the energy going toward Alzheimer's drugs.

item.title: Are Micro Social Interactions the Antidote to Loneliness?
item.description:
Loneliness

Are Micro Social Interactions the Antidote to Loneliness?

During a loneliness epidemic, small interactions can connect us.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that "micro interactions" like making small talk can carry psychological benefits.
  • Micro interactions are positively correlated with happiness and can combat feelings of loneliness.
  • Social media and a lack of gathering spaces has worsened loneliness, but everyday connections can help.

Recently, I stopped at a local brewery with the intention of just having one drink and a few moments of peace. I ended up getting into a discussion with the bartender, and we talked at length about books, writers, and literature. He made a few book recommendations, as did I, and we had a truly nice conversation that was engaging, reciprocal, and warm. For the time I was there, it felt less like a transactional relationship between customer and server, and more like two friends connecting on common interests. I am currently reading one of the books he recommended, finding it interesting and feeling grateful for having had the opportunity to hear his thoughts and to learn about an author with whom I had not been familiar.

This type of interaction, when viewed psychologically, is termed a “minimal social interaction” or “a micro interaction,” clinical ways to describe everyday social encounters and interactions. Surprisingly, there is an extensive body of research to show that these types of seemingly small and meaningless interactions actually carry vast positive psychological benefits. I can attest that my mood had noticeably improved following my conversation at the brewery; I felt a sense of connectedness and joy in having had the opportunity to talk about a topic that I find truly interesting with an engaged participant.

These beneficial “micro interactions” can be even smaller than the one I describe; encounters like brief exchanges with a store clerk, small talk with a stranger while waiting in line, or exchanging a quick laugh with another parent at a playground, for instance, can reap big benefits. According to a study in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, “even social interactions with the more peripheral members of our social networks contribute to our well-being” (Sandstrom & Dunn, 2014). A 2023 study that aimed to replicate earlier findings about the benefits of micro interactions concluded that “minimal social interaction was positively correlated with happiness and the effects of minimal social interaction were significantly mediated by loneliness, a measure of sense of belonging” (Ishiguro, 2023).

At a time when the statistics on loneliness are staggering—the World Health Organization (WHO) reports that globally, one in six individuals experience loneliness and the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) report that in the United States, one in four adults feel they do not have the social network they need—anything we can do to combat what is increasingly being referred to as a “loneliness epidemic” should be considered (CDC, 2024; WHO, 2025). Micro interactions are a simple, accessible way to take small steps to reduce feelings of loneliness and isolation.

Psychologically speaking, the idea of belongness is not new: Alfred Maslow, in his 1943 “Hierarchy of Needs,” positioned “love and belonging needs” as a foundational level of adaptive human functioning, following only physiological needs and safety needs (Maslow, 1943). Human beings literally need connection, reciprocity, and relationships to survive, but our current time presents a great challenge as we find ourselves more separated, divided, and isolated than ever before. While it would be wonderful if we could all surround ourselves with countless friends and large social groups, the reality is that we face many barriers, from social media isolation to a lack of gathering spaces to discrimination and marginalization.

In the face of a big problem, small steps often have a larger impact than we think. Making an effort to increase our micro social interactions—a deceptively small step—can help to combat the pervasive sense of loneliness and isolation that so many of us feel these days.

item.title: Fashion and Fertility
item.description:
Beauty

Fashion and Fertility

Women are more interested in designer labels when fertile.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Women's behavior changes during the fertile phase of their cycle in ways that may attract men.
  • Women are more interested in designer label clothing and accessories when fertile.
  • This pattern only emerges when women judge items for themselves, not for other women.
  • Desire for luxury goods may be part of a two-stage tactic of attracting high-quality partners.
Source: Joanna Malinowska / Freestocks

Evolutionary psychologists have long been interested in the connection between fertility and behavior. Many studies have shown that during the most fertile phase of the ovulatory cycle (the few days after ovulation), women behave in ways that appear likely to increase their success in the mating market.

Women are judged more physically attractive when fertile. This may be because of physical changes (for example, psychologists have tested whether a woman’s position in her cycle affects her skin color and even her breast symmetry) or because of differences in what is sometimes called ornamentation: the clothes and accessories a woman chooses to wear. In fact, researchers have shown that when most fertile, women tend to prefer to wear more revealing clothing.

But clothing can appeal to potential partners for reasons other than how much skin it reveals. Recently, a team of consumer and management psychologists from the U.S. and South Korea, led by Aekyoung Kim of Jeonbuk National University, set out to discover whether hormonal fluctuations associated with fertility affect women’s desire for luxury clothing brands.

The psychologists acknowledge that their investigation may seem counterintuitive given that men are not often thought to find women who wear designer clothing particularly attractive. Standard accounts of mate preferences based on evolutionary theory note that women tend to find cues to a man’s wealth attractive because our female ancestors fared better when they secured investment from their male partners: their children were more likely to survive to reproductive age. Our male ancestors, however, were less interested in securing investment, because the most efficient way for a man to increase his reproductive success was to acquire more partners. Luxury clothing is a conspicuous marker of wealth, so why should men find it attractive?

Kim and her colleagues observe that women may wear luxury clothing as a way of drawing attention to themselves. This is important because, after all, a man can’t be attracted to a woman unless he notices her first. Of course, there are cheaper ways of being noticed than springing for a Burberry purse or a pair of Louboutin shoes, but the psychologists note that luxury clothing and accessories may have a generally positive effect, making a woman feel more confident and therefore attractive.

They also make the case that women may operate a two-stage strategy when it comes to finding a partner. In the first stage, women seek to attract a large pool of appealing admirers; in the second, they choose from this pool their preferred partner. Luxury clothing may be a component of the first stage of this strategy. Such clothing may project prestige, which draws in similarly prestigious men while simultaneously warning less-prestigious men to steer clear: a way of saying without words, “You’re not in my league.”

Kim and colleagues had young women come to their lab and provide a urine sample for hormone testing. In combination with answers to questions about their cycles, the results of these hormone tests could be used to determine whether a woman was in the fertile or non-fertile phase. Women attended the lab twice: once when in the high fertility and once when in the low fertility phase. At the lab, they took part in an innovative experiment. They were given a sheet of paper showing images of a handbag and a pair of shoes, as well as examples of various designer label logos (Gucci, Chanel, Louis Vuitton). They were then asked to draw one of these logos onto the images of the accessories, imagining that these would be items they could take home with them.

The psychologists then measured the size of the logos drawn by each participant. They found that women drew larger logos during the fertile as opposed to the non-fertile phase of their cycles. When women were asked to imagine that they were creating accessories for another woman to take home, they drew smaller logos during the fertile phase as opposed to the non-fertile phase.

These findings imply that women prefer more conspicuous shows of luxury when fertile, but only for themselves. The fact that fertile women wanted other women’s displays to be less extravagant is suggestive of intrasexual competition: women seeking to outshine their potential rivals in love.

In a second experiment, the psychologists had women express their preferences for high- and low-end T-shirt brands, imagining that they were purchasing the items to be worn mostly in public or in private. The results of this experiment supported the first: Women in the fertile phase of their cycles had a greater desire to purchase luxury brands to be consumed in public rather than in private.

Kim and colleagues believe that their results will be useful to marketers. In their peer-reviewed article, published in the journal PLOS One, they note that brands could benefit from targeting advertisements for luxury products at women during the high-fertility phase of their cycles: “At the very least, luxury brands should be more aware that the women being exposed to their marketing efforts face hormonal changes and be strategic about how to position their products based on how these changes influence desires and behaviors.”

The psychologists acknowledge that some luxury brands use small or hidden logos, and therefore do not conspicuously advertise their wearers’ wealth (at least to those not in the know). They also note that “there are contexts and communities in which luxury is simply not appreciated, in general, and we do not claim that our findings would apply in these contexts.”

item.title: What Does Good Followership Look Like?
item.description:
Leadership

What Does Good Followership Look Like?

A guide for team members, followers, and leaders.

Posted September 29, 2026

I was recently asked to provide some comments at the Global Followership Conference held this past summer at Indiana Wesleyan University. In addition to answering some questions, I provided some guidelines for what good followership looks like. Here is a summary.

Q. When a leader delegates responsibility to a follower, that comes with accepting the risks. In other words, there are benefits, but also real costs. What are your thoughts?

A. Responsibility comes with risks and obligations. As a leader, you can’t delegate control and responsibility effectively if you still “control the shots.” As a follower who is empowered, you have to accept the responsibility and realize the weight of that and accept the consequences and the outcomes.

It is clear that there can be real costs. We might reframe leaders of social movements as actually being “followers” who are resisting the status quo. Therefore, Nelson Mandela is not a leader initially. He is a follower who resists, and has to pay the price — 27 years of imprisonment. In the workplace, an empowered follower who takes on this responsibility must also consider the consequences, which can be positive or negative.

Q. One of the persistent tensions in followership is the difference between healthy support and unhealthy compliance. From a psychological perspective, what helps people discern when loyalty is virtuous and when loyalty has become complicity?

A. The key is that followers need to understand their role — including the power that they have to resist, if necessary. It means not just acquiescing, but keeping your eyes open; analyzing; being critical in one’s evaluation of situations. Critical thinking is a key foundational construct in human psychology.

Barbara Kellerman, in her recent book, Why We Follow Leaders, and Why We Don’t, states that submission is the human condition (she draws on evolutionary theory, psychology, ethology). Submission and obedience are the follower “default” system. The point is that it is very hard NOT to just follow. As followership expert, Ira Chaleff, emphasizes, it takes courage to resist leaders (and it also takes courage to follow and support leaders who themselves are meeting resistance).

The key is that followers need to understand their role — including the power that they have to resist, if necessary. It means not just acquiescing, but keeping your eyes open; analyzing; being critical in one’s evaluation of situations. Critical thinking is a key foundational construct in human psychology.

It is also important for followers (and leaders) to understand the dynamics of the situation — the context in which the collective exists. We can’t truly understand “leadership” without understanding the leader, the follower, and the situation/context. Unfortunately, we don’t often think of the situational variables in operation that affect both leadership and followership. That includes the cultural elements, the history of the collective [think the 250-year history of the U.S.], the norms and patterns of behavior and actions, the relationship dynamics, and many more variables.

Q. What does a psychologically mature follower look like in practice, not just behaviorally, but cognitively, emotionally, relationally, and ethically?

Cognitively

  • Exercises independent thinking
  • Is an active contributor to decision making and to operations
  • Understands the dynamics of the collective — the leader-followers relationship
  • Accepts responsibility and learns from setbacks

Emotionally

  • Shares responsibility for outcomes and especially failures
  • Is temperate; Maintains composure
  • Is emotionally intelligent (although I’m not a big fan of some of the “kitchen sink” models of EI)
  • Is courageous (partly emotional, partly cognitive)

Relationally

  • Takes responsibility for building high-quality relationships with leaders, peers, and subordinates
  • Is socially intelligent and socially skilled
  • Is an active support for the leader when the leader is engaged in mission-consistent courses of action

Ethically

  • Has the moral courage to confront the leader who is engaged in unethical behavior
  • Is committed to the positive values of the collective
  • Analyzes the ethicality of courses of action
  • Is a person of good, virtuous character (this is also critical for leaders [and every member of the collective])
  • Is fair and just in dealing with self and others
  • Is ethically responsible

item.title: An Attitude Change Regarding the Use of Expletives
item.description:
Habit Formation

An Attitude Change Regarding the Use of Expletives

What may explain our national increase in the use of expletives?

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Expletives are processed by different brain circuits than ordinary speech.
  • Expletives can become so automated and habitual that they defy the most vigorous efforts to suppress them.
  • Expletives may help with favorably altering bodily and emotional responses.

Many of us are more or less likely to utter expletives on occasions when we are frustrated, impatient, or angry. But some people seem to employ expletives even in their most serene of mental states.

Expletive derives from the Latin word expletivus, which means “serving to take up space” and usually refers principally to overlearned and sometimes highly emotionally charged words. The use of expletives traditionally has been considered verboten except in informal conversations among intimates. This strict distinction separating expletives from acceptable speech can be traced back at least as recently as the transcription of Richard Nixon’s Oval Office tapes, in which the phrase “expletive deleted” confirmed the mores of the time. We’ve undergone quite a change since then in terms of what’s tolerated, if not wholly acceptable, regarding the use of expletives.

During a Senate Homeland Security & Government Affairs Meeting on July 29, 2026, Senator Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) described a 2020 incident when an Ohio mother was arrested for refusing to wear a mask at a middle school football game. Senator Moreno asked the witness, Dr. Anthony Fauci, “Here I’m sitting in front of you six years later saying, who the f*ck do you think you were for doing that?”

When a formerly “deleted” term rises to the rank of acceptable civil discourse within the United States Senate, its use in less august circumstances becomes easily understandable. But rather than employing expletives simply as a filler, some people seem to greatly overwork them, as in a conversation I recently overheard while sitting in a coffee shop: “I arrived for our f*cking meeting and he wasn’t there. I then decided I wasn’t going to f*cking hang around all f*cking day. I was thinking of f*cking calling him, but then I thought: F*ck him. I’m going to f*cking take myself back to the f*cking dorm.”

For such people, the use of expletives becomes so automated and habitual that, like all habits, it becomes very difficult to break. One avenue to controlling the use of expletives (but only if one is interested in doing so!) comes from examining the brain’s role in their formation and expression.

Neurobiology of Expletives

First, expletives can be expressed either voluntarily or involuntarily, with both involving a highly practiced lingual-motor sequence. When the swearing is voluntary, a decision precedes the expletive. Involuntary swearing is both more common and more revealing of the underlying brain mechanisms. One specific expletive known as coprolalia (the compulsion to speak expletives in the presence of other people) involves the urge to shout out “bad words” competing against the simultaneous desire to suppress the words. In the neurologic illness Tourette syndrome, this inner tension between saying and not saying can lead to a frenzied paralysis of will based on the simultaneous affirmation and negation of coprolalic words.

A useful way to understand an expletive is to consider it, like all words, as a symbol. But it’s a symbol linking motor-speech patterns with emotion and social tolerance and intolerance stemming from a person’s earliest years when subtle and often not so subtle prohibitions (and if necessary punishments) were employed to discourage children from expressing themselves in words that their parents judged to be crude, obscene, or otherwise objectionable.

Based on imaging studies, neuroscientists have demonstrated that the brain circuits involved in Tourette’s, as well as other repetitive uses of expletives, include the basal ganglia, thalamus, motor areas, cingulate cortex, and prefrontal inhibitory system. When functioning normally, the circuit prevents the expletive from reaching its vocal expression thanks to the inhibitory effect of the prefrontal cortex.

As a result of the specialized neuronal network empowering it, an expletive may survive neurologic damage that adversely impacts the pathways responsible for normal everyday language. Thanks to the resulting aphasia (a language and communication disorder affecting the ability to enunciate), the aphasic person’s speech may become grievously impaired; in some instances it may consist only of short guttural, largely incomprehensible attempts at words.

In this context, expletives become an alternative means of communication. The result is often both tragic and poignant. A clergyman I once cared for after a stroke spoke principally in expletives. What was worse, whenever he heard himself speak these words, he became agitated, depressed, and overcome by his inability to suppress them. His agonizing dilemma was based on the following:

Damage to his left hemisphere, which contains the speech centers, interfered with his ability to speak using expletives: A reliable indicator that expletives are stored and retrieved via a different brain circuitry than for normal speech. The right hemisphere and the underlying subcortical system are both important for what’s called formulaic language: words that have been heard or spoken so often over the years that they become overlearned, such as a person’s name, phrases taken from prayers, lines from the National Anthem, clichés, “small talk,” automatic phrases (“thank you”), and, most importantly, “expletives.”

Of all the formulaic words and phrases in a person’s vocabulary, the brain treats expletives differently by establishing a strong link between the words and the circuits mediating emotions.

This can be traced back to the prohibition which, at least in most families, is directed at discouraging children from expressing themselves in words that are judged crude, obscene, or otherwise objectionable.

So, what may explain our national increase in the use of expletives? For one thing, exposure to expletives and their increasing acceptance roughly parallels the increase in televised streaming services compared to traditional movie-going. Different standards apply in these two technologies. According to the Federal Communications Commission Consumer Guide, “The same rules for indecency and profanity do not apply to cable, satellite TV and satellite radio because they are subscription services.” Thus, the Guide grants streaming services a pass, and if you’ve recently watched streaming productions, you’ll appreciate how extensively that dispensation is being taken advantage of.

Effects of Using Expletives on Bodily and Emotional Responses

But, it turns out, expletives can have some redeeming features, such as favorably altering bodily and emotional responses.

In a now classic experiment measuring how long a person could keep a hand submerged in a bucket of ice-water, 73 percent of the participants who swore during the hand’s submersion increased their time in the frigid water by about 30 seconds.

In another experiment, repeating the word "f*ck" increased the pain threshold to ice water by 32 percent and pain tolerance by 33 percent when compared to participants who repeated words beginning with the letter F, but not expletives.

Unfortunately for the inveterate user of expletives, the favorable effects on pain tolerance eventually disappear. So, too, does the increased activity in the amygdala and prefrontal cortex if the expletive is repeated and repeated seemingly endlessly in a perfunctory manner. In perhaps a form of poetic justice, the habitual user of expletives eventually penalizes only himself: More pain can be expected to be endured in the future, whether he swears or not.

item.title: Sober October Tests Boundaries
item.description:
Boundaries

Sober October Tests Boundaries

Developing discernement may lead to a smaller circle of friends.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Changing your relationship with alcohol isn't simply a matter of willpower.
  • Boundaries are the fences of our psychological life, and discernment is the gatekeeper.
  • Developing discernment naturally leads to a smaller circle of friends.

“I want to, but when I attempted Dry January, I felt so alone,” a client said when I suggested he take part in Sober October.

Changing your relationship with alcohol doesn’t simply require willpower. It’s about understanding the behavioral patterns that trigger you to drink. Regardless of the time of year, I often urge clients who want to change their relationship with alcohol to take a 30-day reset.

Brown University analyzed data from over 150,000 Dry January participants and found that a temporary pause in drinking can lead to meaningful physical and psychological improvements, notably better sleep, improved mood, and meaningful shifts in mental health. Even participants who didn’t abstain entirely still experienced benefits, including improved mental health.

That same review also identified reduced social contact as a side effect. This tracks well with what I hear from clients who wish to change their relationship with alcohol. “Even though I explained I wouldn’t be drinking for one month," the same client said, "my friends still encouraged me to drink or ordered a drink for me despite my insistence not to. I ended up succumbing to peer pressure.”

This form of boundary crossing is not uncommon.

Building Fences, Not Walls

Boundaries are the fences of our psychological life, and discernment is the gatekeeper. Discernment is the wisdom that helps you decide when to open the gate and when to lock it. It is the quality of being perceptive and exercising keen judgment to separate what is true, important, or right from what is false or trivial. This concept, described by Henry Cloud and John Townsend in Boundaries (1992), has always fascinated me. It is one of the most difficult concepts to grasp, especially for those raised in households that encouraged them to “keep the peace,” “not to ruffle feathers,” or “don’t make waves.”

The result is people-pleasing adults who expend tremendous energy maintaining the status quo at the expense of their own needs. Even if an individual learns to set boundaries, without discernment, those boundaries become either rigid walls that isolate or porous ones that leave you vulnerable to manipulation. Discernment allows you to build adaptive boundaries based on objective reality. This is crucial for individuals embarking on a journey to better navigate their relationship with alcohol.

When someone crosses the line, pause and evaluate the situation. Did they intentionally disrespect you, or do they lack self-awareness? Your boundary response changes based on this distinction. A useful way to assess this is through trial and error: how someone reacts when you set a minor boundary tells you how they will handle a bigger one, or what essentially comes down to respect versus guilt-tripping.

Developing discernment naturally leads to a smaller circle of friends because it shifts your priority from quantity to quality. You stop evaluating friendships based on metrics. Instead, you start to evaluate friends based on character, safety, and mutual alignment.

If you're trying Sober October for the first time, think of it as an experiment. Stay curious and document how sobriety affects your sleep, mood, and social life. The key question is what role you want alcohol to play in your life and which relationships support your decision.

item.title: How Ordinary Things Become Sexual Fetishes
item.description:
Sex

How Ordinary Things Become Sexual Fetishes

Pavlov’s dogs, a pair of boots, and three surprising first experiences.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus becomes linked with a bodily response through repeated pairing.
  • Classical conditioning is an essential component of how fetishes develop.
  • One stimulating experience during a critical stage in sexual development can be enough to create a fetish.

One day in the 1890s, the Russian scientist Ivan Pavlov rang a bell to call his dogs for dinner—I like to imagine that this was standard for 19th-century dog owners, those classy rascals—and noticed that they had drenched themselves in their own slobber. He was about to roll his eyes with playful indignation when he realized that he hadn’t even brought the food out yet! If not the smell of the food, what were they slobbering over? He ran some tests. Turns out, it was the bell. More tests, and he found out that they would slobber over anything at all that fell into one of two categories: (a) food and (b) once-random things that they had come to associate with food. This doesn’t sound mind-blowing at first, but it is. Pats on the head, flicks to the ear, a song, a “Woop Woop Time to Eat”—repeatedly pair anything with food, and that thing will eventually be able to make dogs slobber, no food needed.

How Classical Conditioning Works

As you may have already gathered, this phenomenon also applies to people in a big way. In fact, this pervasive psychological principle explains why the smell of coffee wakes you up, why the Netflix “duh-DUN” sound triggers instant relaxation, and why you can’t hang around with guys named Jim no more. Classical conditioning works like this: A neutral stimulus (like a sound, smell, or sight) becomes associated with a bodily response through repeated pairing with a significant event. After enough pairings, your brain starts reacting to the neutral stimulus as though it were the significant event.

So, for example, your phone ding triggers excitement because in the past it has been paired with sexy texts from cute boys or loving texts from your friends. Your body has a positive emotional reaction based on what has come after that sound in the past. For those overworked souls who use their phones primarily for professional purposes, that same neutral ding might precipitate abject dread. The ding is neither your boss nor that hot dude; it’s just a ding. Your brain, though, associates them so closely that your body reacts in the same way to the ding that it would to the real message from that potent person.

Classical conditioning is an essential component of how fetishes develop. In the 1960s, a few inspired researchers paired classical conditioning with sexiness. In one experiment, heterosexual male participants were first shown an image of boots, which—I’m here to report—are not very sexy for most people.¹ Immediately after seeing the boots, they were shown images of naked women, which, naturally, perked them right up. After enough pairings, the boots alone began to elicit sexual arousal. The participants’ brains had linked the sight of boots with the feeling of arousal that accompanied the naked women. After enough pairings, the boots elicited a similar level of sexual response to the naked women! A nice pair of boobs—boots—was all these fine gentlemen now needed to get excited. Even weeks later, the boot-boob pairing had lessened but had not disappeared. Another study found the same results with pennies, showing that almost anything can become sexualized when it’s paired with breasts—even something as mundane and unsexy as pennies. (Dollar bills, this researcher acknowledges, are a different story.)²

Fetish Development

Many of the wonderful humans who are my clients talk about their fetishes as having sprung from a childhood experience that paired intense sexuality with something random. We refer to this phenomenon as sexual conditioning. Although sexual conditioning often develops after several pairings, if someone has a particularly stimulating experience during a critical stage in sexual development, one incident can be enough to create a fetish.

For example, a survey respondent with a foot fetish shared, “There was a girl who lived down the road from me—she was a bit older—and she would always walk around barefoot when we hung out. One day while we were hanging out at her house, she started rubbing her feet on my penis under the covers. It was then I knew I loved women’s feet.” Nothing like a good rubdown to forever link feet with pleasure.

Coincidences are the lifeblood of sexual conditioning, as unexpected encounters coming at just the right moment can forever fuse just about anything with sexual arousal. One woman, let’s call her Katie, who filled out my fetish survey said, “I think it was just a coincidence that my first exposure to anything related to a penis was a video of a guy peeing, and that made me associate the two and develop a fetish for it.” Another classic example of sexual conditioning came from a respondent, let’s call him Matt, with a fulsome and satisfying latex fetish: “I remember being a teenager and seeing a condom machine in a gas station bathroom. They were fifty cents at the time. I got one, thinking if I wore it, then I would know what sex felt like. That was not exactly the case, but I did develop a massive fetish for latex.” Classical conditioning lends the weight of science to the old adage that we all know to be true: You never forget your first time.

item.title: Perception, Psychedelics, and the Lap of Consciousness
item.description:
Consciousness

Perception, Psychedelics, and the Lap of Consciousness

What psychedelic journeys and contemplative practice reveal about awareness.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Profound experiences, chemical or contemplative, reveal we are part of something far larger.
  • A single opening can set the path. Maintaining it takes practice: yoga, meditation, self inquiry.
  • Cessation and pure presence studies show complex brain activity even when reportable experience is suspended.

Michael Pollan spent most of his career writing about food and plants. Then the plants and the return of his gaze led him somewhere unexpected. In How to Change Your Mind, he describes a series of profound experiences, moments in which he felt something beyond his mind and body, and the question those moments set in motion: What is consciousness, and what are we within it? He interviewed scientists, therapists, and fellow travelers. He went far beyond journalism. He experienced it himself.

Is that not what draws so many people to psychedelics? For a few hours, the boundaries soften. People report touching something beyond mind and body, and they return with a humbling recognition: I am a small piece of this planet, and something far larger is operating here.

The Doorway and Its Limits

A single experience of that kind, if it sets a person on the right path, may be enough to begin. It can reorganize priorities, dissolve old certainties, and open a genuine curiosity about what lies beyond the ordinary mind.

But here is the honest question: How do you maintain it?

What I think of as consciousness hygiene is not built in one night. Living from that place rather than merely visiting it requires sustained practice: yoga, meditation, breath, and self-inquiry. The contemplative traditions that mapped these territories thousands of years ago never treated the profound experience as the destination. They treated it as the invitation.

The Science Is Catching Up

Research frameworks now exist for questions that were once purely philosophical. Giulio Tononi's Integrated Information Theory offers one rigorous account of what consciousness might be and how to measure it. Provocative new perspectives are arriving from physics and from computational science, and these frameworks can guide the next generation of experiments.

The empirical findings are just as striking. Researchers at Massachusetts General Hospital studying advanced meditators in extended cessation, periods in which reportable experience is temporarily suspended, have found that the brain during these states shows complex, organized activity rather than a simple shutdown. Something structured persists even when ordinary experience does not. And in our own published work, brainwave changes begin within two to three minutes of simple breath-watching meditation and peak at seven minutes, even in people who have never meditated before (Mindfulness, 2026).

These findings point to a larger, humbling framework. Consciousness appears to be far bigger than the contents of any individual mind.

The Lap of Consciousness

We have been gifted an extraordinary cerebral cortex, advanced enough to ask a question no other creature can ask: Do we produce consciousness, or can we touch a dimension of consciousness that is already there? Science has not settled this. It may be the deepest open question we have.

The realized masters of the contemplative traditions, such as Sadhguru, approach it from the other direction. They invite us to realize the context of our lives, not merely manage the content. In that framing, each of us is a small pop-up appearing in a vast lap of consciousness, in which, through which, and with which we experience everything.

We do not have to resolve the theory to test the invitation.

It Comes Down to Attention

Sadhguru teaches that when there is undivided attention without intention, existence yields. When it yields, experience becomes profound. And when there is profoundness of experience, transformation follows on its own. Compassion flows as a consequence, not a commandment. For society at large, this may be the most practical implication of all: Profound experience is the doorway to self-transformation, and self-transformation changes how we treat each other and this planet.

A Doorway Without a Substance

For those who want to test this without a substance, there is a simple place to begin. The Miracle of Mind app offers a free, guided seven-minute meditation created by Sadhguru, the same style of breath-watching practice our EEG research has studied.

One finding from this work is quietly remarkable. In a study of 1,325 participants, now accepted and in press at BMC Psychology, a single seven-minute session changed how people rated their feelings over the previous month. The month itself had not changed. Not one event in it was different. What changed was perception.

Everything remains the same. The way you see it does not have to.

That is the beginning: to see everything the way it is. Not through tinted glasses. Through clear lenses.

item.title: Recalled to Life by Naloxone (Narcan)
item.description:
Addiction

Recalled to Life by Naloxone (Narcan)

OSHA wants more: The Narcan kit needs to be within reach; treatment must follow.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • OSHA urges workplaces to stock naloxone, train workers, and keep kits easy to find.
  • Naloxone reverses opioid overdose, but someone must recognize the emergency and reach the kit in time.
  • Families, campuses, and workplaces need naloxone within reach—and someone knowing how to use it.
  • Rescue is the first step. Survivors also need evaluation, addiction treatment, and help staying in treatment.

Naloxone (Narcan) is a lifesaving nasal spray reversing potentially fatal opioid overdoses. It’s a scarily good drug because an overdose reversal is often the difference between life and death. In 1987, I highlighted Narcan in my book Wonder Drugs as a powerful, life-saving pharmaceutical antidote capable of rapidly reversing opioid overdoses.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) provisionally estimated 69,973 overdose deaths in 2025, substantially down from 81,313 in 2024. Naloxone has saved many lives, though changes in fentanyl drug supply, treatment, and prevention also contributed to the decline. It is a remarkable success in an area with too few of them. From September 2018 through March 2023, state opioid response programs reported distributing more than 8 million kits and more than 500,000 overdose reversals.

On September 24, 2026, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) advised employers nationwide to make naloxone accessible at work, to teach employees to recognize an overdose, to show them how to use the drug, and to place kits where people can find them. That’s good on you, OSHA. Note: OSHA’s naloxone fact sheet is advisory, not a workplace requirement.

We prepare for other medical emergencies. An automated external defibrillator hangs on employers’ walls because cardiac arrest doesn’t wait for an ambulance. Allergic people at risk of anaphylaxis carry their own epinephrine, even when school/workplaces keep some on hand.

Naloxone belongs at work, but the workplace kit cannot follow someone home. The family kit cannot help someone overdosing across the factory floor. CDC also advises people at increased risk of opioid overdose to carry the drug with them and keep another kit at home.

We Know Naloxone Works

Naloxone reverses breathing suppression caused by opioids. Someone recognizes a likely or possible overdose, accesses the medication, and administers the nasal spray. They also call 911 and continue to support breathing until emergency help arrives.

A 2025 review of community naloxone programs found high survival rates after reported administration: 98.3 percent continued their lives in programs serving people using drugs, 95.0 percent in programs serving families and community members, and 92.4 percent in police programs. These percentages don’t include people who overdosed alone at home or for whom the kit arrived too late.

Years before today’s decline in overdose deaths, Allison Pitt, Keith Humphreys, and Margaret Brandeau at Stanford modeled responses to the opioid epidemic. They projected that expanding naloxone use would save the most lives in the near term. But their caution was prescient: There were many things that we should do to reverse the opioid death crisis, but no single policy would solve this epidemic. We needed everything: rescue, treatment, and prevention. Still do.

Who Has Naloxone Now?

A 2025 review found studies of occupational naloxone training focused heavily on healthcare workers and first responders. In a survey of commercial fishing vessel captains, 10 of 61 had received naloxone training. Five vessels carried it. Let’s make sure Narcan is accessible at most workplaces, increasing the odds of access and life versus death.

Massachusetts studies subsequently associated wider naloxone distribution with lower opioid overdose death rates or more favorable death-rate trends.

Ontario went further than OSHA. Since 2023, employers must provide a kit and training if they know, or should know, that a worker could overdose at work. Scotland reports its national take-home naloxone program reached an estimated 82.2 percent of people at risk in 2024–25; frontline police and ambulance staff also carry it. Program reach does not mean everyone has a kit. But someone is likely within reach.

Now consider a college residence hall at 2 a.m. In a 2026 study of 237 four-year public colleges, 28 percent operated campus naloxone distribution programs. That doesn't mean others did nothing. But it could mean that. It also raises a better question: Can a roommate, resident adviser, or campus police officer access Narcan for an overdosing student in time?

Airplanes? The FAA says several major U.S. airlines carry naloxone and has proposed making opioid-overdose response part of required in-flight medical capability. But this is an old problem that should have been addressed by now. Jessi Gold, MD, MS, wrote about what happens without naloxone in an overdose on an airplane in 2018. How about taking action, now or soon?

Concert venues are beginning to organize overdose training. What about the next stadium or arena you visit? Who has naloxone? How long would it take to reach a fan with Narcan? “Medical staff on site” sounds good. So does “defibrillator in the building.” Neither answers the question about who can help and where the Narcan kit is when the clock is ticking, and it’s minutes to death from overdose.

The Person Receives Narcan, Waking Up Alive. Now What?

Naloxone restores breathing. It doesn’t treat opioid use disorder (OUD), but provides future opportunities for treatment. I recently wrote about the trapdoor after opioid reversal. In a Medicare study of 136,762 survivors of nonfatal drug overdoses, only 4.1 percent received medication for OUD (MOUD) within a year. In another national cohort, only 8.8 percent of people who started the MOUD treatment medication buprenorphine after an emergency overdose reversal stayed on the drug for six months.

After maintaining life, a workplace or campus plan should try to help facilitate addiction treatment: medication when appropriate, and an appointment with someone who can see the person and help them stay in care. A telephone number to call is not a warm handoff and is not enough.

Naloxone may not reverse a person’s problems with thinking. Persistent confusion after breathing resumes deserves medical and neurological evaluation. Ask about past overdoses and Narcan rescues; it’s important to know because added-on cognitive injury can make an already-difficult recovery even harder.

Naloxone reverses opioid effects, not effects of alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, or methamphetamine. When opioids may be involved, administer it, call 911, and support breathing until help arrives. Give another dose if breathing has not returned after two to three minutes. Demi Lovato received naloxone and emergency care after her overdose. She later described lasting injuries. Rescue mattered. It was only the beginning. If the person didn’t take opioids, naloxone won’t hurt them.

Put naloxone at work and home, on the fishing boat, on the plane, at a concert or sporting event, or wherever, and on college campuses. Encourage families and friends of people with substance use disorders and drug use issues to carry the drug. Then ask the questions OSHA’s announcement cannot yet answer: Where is the kit? Who is trained in using it?

Naloxone can save a life today, and we should be grateful for this "second chance," an opportunity to be recalled or brought back to life. But tomorrow requires a plan.

item.title: Would You Work at Starbucks for Free?
item.description:
Motivation

Would You Work at Starbucks for Free?

What makes one unpaid task feel meaningful and another feel absurd?

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Meaning can transform how we experience the same activity.
  • External rewards can sometimes reduce intrinsic motivation.
  • Giving back can create purpose, connection, and a sense that we matter.

Let me ask you this. Would you volunteer your time at a soup kitchen? Providing food and beverages to those who are hungry and thirsty. And, if you said yes, how would that make you feel to give your time for this cause without pay?

Now, let me ask you this. Would you volunteer your time at a Starbucks? Providing food and beverages to those who are hungry and thirsty. And if you said no, why? The big question we should be asking ourselves is: Why can two activities that look almost identical (handing food and drinks to strangers) feel completely different to us?

What motivates us?

We are motivated to do what we love, and we don't need anything external such as money, a promotion, or recognition to do it. Think about reading, crossword puzzles, playing a sport, running, or anything else you love to do. You do them because you enjoy them and this form of motivation drives us to do things that we are passionate about.

Pay decreases our desire to do them. This is because pay is an extrinsic motivator and it sucks the passion right out of the activity, making it a task, job, requirement, and often a burden. Take any passion and add pay or a requirement to get something (a promotion or grade) and the motivation completely shifts. If you love to read and were suddenly reading for pay, each book becomes a box to check off, and you might try to read faster and not enjoy it as much because your motivation shifts from taking in the story to completing a task.

The surprise

Rewards (or extrinsic motivation) don't always increase our motivation to do things. In fact, rewards, money, awards, and recognition can actually decrease our desire to do something we previously enjoyed. Imagine reading for pleasure and then being paid to review each book you read. You may end up reading less. Your once pleasurable activity can become a "job".

The bigger idea is meaning

We don't experience the activities we are engaged in solely based on the physical aspects of doing it. Like serving food to needy individuals. We don't simply think of the act of serving. We think of how it makes us feel. We do it because we feel like we are doing something of value. Our activity has a purpose that is bigger than the physical act of doing it. We experience it according to why we believe we are doing it.

How can we harness intrinsic motivation in real life?

Intrinsic motivation isn't just good for us in the obvious ways that it motivates us to do things we enjoy, it helps us to give back to others, contributing to the greater good. We are built to tap into our intrinsic motivation, especially in midlife, to give back to others, creating a legacy and feeling that we matter in the world. Some examples of using intrinsic motivation to give back might include volunteering, engaging in activities that support a cause, and mentoring.

The next time you find yourself losing interest in something you once loved doing, ask yourself what changed. Did the activity change? Or, did your reason for doing it change? It just might be that intrinsic motivation shifted to extrinsic motivation. It may not be the activity, but the meaning you attribute to why you are doing it.

item.title: How to Persuade Without Being a Creep
item.description:
Persuasion

How to Persuade Without Being a Creep

Why attention to morality can make us better persuaders.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Being focused on persuasion can be morally off-putting.
  • Being respectful can increase others' motivation to hear us out.
  • On polarizing topics, small exchanges can be the start of bigger shifts.

Imagine you’ve got a date at a coffee shop. You decide to bring a book, just in case the other person is late. But what kind of book? A novel? Nonfiction? Keep in mind that your date will probably see it.

There’s no single right answer, of course. But here’s a piece of advice: Don’t bring a book on the psychology of persuasion. It doesn’t matter whether it’s Dale Carnegie’s classic, How to Win Friends and Influence People, or a contemporary, research-driven book like Robert Cialdini’s Influence or Tali Sharot’s The Influential Mind. Those are great reads, but if your date sees you reading them, they might turn around and walk out the door. Why? Because you’d probably look like a creep.

Manipulation

A creep is willing to manipulate other people, using tricks to lure them into doing unsavory things. Creeps reach into our private lives in ways they shouldn’t, and that includes trying to work our psychology. That isn’t just impolite—it’s morally off-putting.

Don’t get me wrong: A little manipulation doesn’t automatically make you a creep. In fact, there are contexts where we’re OK with some manipulation. We generally put up with advertisements, which are often a bit manipulative. Or, to take another example, one aspiring commercial real estate agent told me that commercial real estate was a “blood sport,” where psychological maneuvering was just part of the game. Those are special cases, though. In other contexts, showing too much interest in persuasive tricks can get you in trouble.

I’m a professor of ethics and philosophy at the University of Washington, where I teach a class called Philosophy 118: “The Ethics and Psychology of Persuasion.” The students who sign up all want to become more persuasive, and some of them are headed for careers in marketing or commercial real estate. But most of them also want to persuade friends and family members, and they want to do that without being creepy. They want to avoid manipulative tricks and to preserve their moral integrity.

Respectful Persuasion

Fortunately, that kind of persuasion is possible. In Phil 118, we read work by ethicists such as George Tsai and Regina Rini, alongside selected pieces of social psychology. My students come to realize that respectful persuasion actually can work, and that it can be far more effective than most forms of manipulation.

Here’s one example. As psychologists such as Shelly Chaiken and Richard Petty argued decades ago, the most lasting, powerful forms of persuasion happen when people really think through an issue, appreciate the arguments, and put the pieces together themselves. But life is busy, and people can’t think through everything that comes up. As a result, powerful persuasion happens only when someone has two things: motivation to think things through and enough bandwidth to do it.

This is where ethics comes in. The great German philosopher Immanuel Kant argued that moral respect required a few things: sincerity, an openness to learn, and a willingness to give others space to live their lives. To persuade someone respectfully, then, you need to sincerely make your case, give them a chance to teach you something, and—most importantly—do all this at a time and place that works for the other person.

Here’s how this pans out in my class. My students reach out to somebody whom they know they disagree with and ask, “Can I try to respectfully persuade you?” They then have to find a good time and space to do this, and ask the other person to score them on how respectful they are. All that setup sets the stage for deep, effective persuasion: By showing respect, my students provide motivation for other people to hear them out, and by finding a good setting, they make sure that the other people have bandwidth to think things through.

I don’t want to oversell this: A single conversation rarely totally changes someone’s mind, even when it’s respectful. But the results I’ve seen are still pretty amazing: One student told me that she changed her father’s mind about student debt forgiveness—and that it was their first productive political conversation. Other students had productive exchanges with friends who disagreed with them about ICE deportations. None of their friends instantly flipped, but many of them walked away with a more nuanced understanding of the issue. In our current age of hyper-polarization, that’s pretty encouraging.

This is only part of what my students and I have discovered together about ethical persuasion. We’ve also found insights by looking carefully at the approaches of master persuaders, such as Nobel Prize winner Jane Addams, who was key to the women’s suffrage movement, and the musician Daryl Davis, who has convinced dozens of members of the KKK to leave the Klan. We also learn about various biases and how people can navigate those without sacrificing self-respect. The ultimate lesson, though, is that some successful persuaders are committed to respect, compassion, and other moral values—and those values actually make them more effective. When persuasion is guided by both ethics and psychology, there’s nothing creepy about it.

(I distill some insights from my class in Just Hear Me Out: How to Change Minds Without Lies, Bullsh*t, or Moral Compromise. Bringing that book to a date probably wouldn’t be creepy, but a good novel would probably still be a safer choice.)

item.title: How Can I Get My Anxious Child to Go to Sleep and Stay Asleep?
item.description:
Sleep

How Can I Get My Anxious Child to Go to Sleep and Stay Asleep?

Restoring sleep for you and your kid.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • The majority of kids with anxiety disorders have disruptions in sleep.
  • You can help your child learn to go to sleep and stay asleep in their own bed.
  • Strategies that help include simplifying your extracurriculars and gradually withdrawing your support.

This post is Part 1 of a series.

Source: Ketut Subiyanto / Pexels

One of the things I dreaded most was a child waking me up in the middle of the night, tapping my shoulder and saying, “Mom, I can’t sleep!” Groggy and confused because I was in the middle of a dream, I then had to gather the energy to either endure the walk back to their bedroom that would then awaken me all the way, or allow them to crawl into bed but allow the very real possibility that I would be kicked awake by their movements while they slept.

I have also repeatedly had sessions that began like this: Two parents and their 4th grader sat across from me in early evening. They all have bags under their eyes and look slightly disheveled. As I talk with the child, I notice one parent’s eyes closing and the other one yawning. While the child answers my questions, the parent with closed eyes nods off. I suspect the other parent will quickly join their partner in slumber. I knew that whatever else I learned, I would most certainly hear about a child who takes way too long to fall asleep and then disrupts the entire family’s sleep when they fail to do so.

Does this sound like your life? Wishing you could get more quality sleep and that your child would do the same? Eighty-five to ninety percent of children and teens with anxiety disorders experience disrupted sleep (Alfano, Ginsburg & Kingery, 2007; Chase & Pincus, 2011). That usually means their parents also experience disrupted sleep because these children are likely to request elaborate bedtime routines, extra contact at bedtime, a preference for sleeping with caretakers, and waking up in the middle of the night to ask to sleep with the parent or to be escorted back to bed, only to resume the request for more comfort to get back to sleep. I often see families with a family bed not by design, but out of desperation, so everyone can get some sleep. I also see partners feeling unjustly ignored because a child is the one cuddled up with the other.

What can be done to help? Here are my top strategies for shifting out of sleep deprivation and into being well-rested.

  1. Simplify your family’s schedule. Too many kids and teens get caught up in sports or arts practices that keep bedtimes late on school nights. Your child needs an hour of wind-down time prior to sleep. Is chronic sleep deprivation the outcome you want for yourself or your child?
  2. Recognize that sleeping with others actually leads to more sleep disruption due to the movements and sounds others make. The same is true for placing nocturnal pets in the bedroom, such as cats, gerbils, hamsters, and ferrets; they are incompatible with human sleep, no matter how much your child loves their pet.
  3. Set a daily bedtime that cannot be violated, and keep the same bedtime on the weekend to ensure predictable, restful sleep.
  4. Create a daily pre-bedtime one-hour wind-down routine of no homework, no sports, just quiet activities, baths or showers, and reading or listening
  5. Use times other than bedtime to catch up and check in with your child. Gradually decrease your support for going to bed and staying in bed. Use a timer and limit reading time, dropping it every few nights until it takes 5-10 minutes for younger children who cannot yet read and 5 minutes or less for readers.
  6. Create an emergency kit: books, picture books, a flashlight that works, a water thermos, pillow mints or antacids, small oyster crackers. Reward for using the emergency kit instead of seeking out parental help.
  7. Always send your kid back to their bed. Your message should be, “You are the one who is best able to put yourself back to sleep, and it is rude to wake others up when you are unable to sleep.”
  8. No negotiating, no matter what they say!
  9. Short and sweet goodnights—one I love you, one hug, and one kiss, and then leave the room without looking back. Make other times during the day your cuddle-up time instead of bedtime.
  10. No exceptions to the short goodnights and tuck-in—not when sick, vomiting, diarrhea, fevers, death of grandparents, divorce—you sleep in your own room and own bed

item.title: Hindsight: The Worst Superpower
item.description:
Self-Talk

Hindsight: The Worst Superpower

So you made a decision that didn’t go to plan? Berate yourself or learn from it.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Ruminating over past mistakes causes shame and anger.
  • With past problems, we often forget crucial elements and instead berate ourselves for making mistakes.
  • Compassion helps us look at past mistakes differently.

Believe it or not, there was once an X-Men character called Hindsight. They could get glimpses of other people’s past just by touching them. Looking back, they probably wished they’d chosen a more helpful power.

I’m not a mutant superhero, but I certainly have lots of regrets. Some big, some small. I remember activities I wish I’d chosen to join and people I wish I’d spoken to (or spoken differently to). I think of purchases I made that ended up being a waste of money. Sadly, there are even choices I made that later caused someone else pain. Currently, I’m in the process of making some big financial decisions, and before it’s even happened, I am imagining future me berating present me for not being able to predict something that went wrong in my imagined future. My mind ruminates over these choices, frustrated that I hadn’t spent more time planning and researching or annoyed that I hadn’t listened to someone else’s advice or just instinctively known that what I was about to do wouldn’t work out. My emotions join in, too; I feel ashamed, angry, and guilty thinking about all the times that things didn’t go to plan.

Source: Simran Sood / Unsplash

But I’m not the only person whose hobby is beating themselves up for not being able to correctly read the future. We all have brains that are problem-solving machines, and these machines work great when the problem is solvable and terribly when the problem has already happened (or hasn’t happened yet). When it comes to solving past problems, brains forget a number of crucial elements and instead just berate us for making mistakes.

Questions to Ask Ourselves

So next time you are giving yourself a hard time because a decision didn’t go the way you wanted it to, ask yourself these questions:

  1. Based on the information you genuinely knew at that time, was there a good likelihood that you would have gotten an outcome you’d wanted?
  2. Based on your previous life experiences, does it make sense that you weren’t sure what the right thing to do was or reached for a strategy that had helped you at another time?
  3. Have you learned from the experience? Will you do something different next time?
  4. Would you be more understanding toward a friend if they had made the same choice you had?

Having Self-Compassion

The answers to these questions may not automatically make you feel better or be any happier about the result of your decision. But maybe the questions will help you have a bit more compassion for past you—that you who felt stuck and had a hard choice to make, and every option had pros and cons, and you had to pick something. And maybe, just maybe, if you have a bit more compassion for yourself, then you’ll spend less time beating yourself up about things you can’t change now and instead can spend more time figuring out what to do next.

Because maybe you, like almost every human, are doing the best that you can with what you’ve got, and being annoyed with yourself for not knowing the answers before you had the chance to fully learn them may not be your best strategy.

And at the same time, I’m sorry that things didn’t go the way you hoped. Good luck from here. This is hard, and you've got this.
