item.title: The Invisible Puberty Happening in Your Teen’s Brain
item.description:
Adolescence

The Invisible Puberty Happening in Your Teen’s Brain

The teen years also bring a neurological puberty.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Teens experience a "neurological puberty," with brain circuits pruned and rebuilt by use.
  • The prefrontal cortex matures last, causing wide variation in teen attention and impulse control.
  • Motivation and autonomy boost teens' willingness to use attention-improving strategies.
  • Letting teens choose focus strategies increases their success and independence over time.
Source: pics five/Shutterstock

The teen brain is not a junior adult brain. It is profoundly different from the brain of either a child or an adult. The most significant of those differences is that the prefrontal cortex, where developing attention/focus networks reside, is the last part of the brain to wire fully into adult levels of efficiency. This is normal development and not pathological. It does, though, sometimes result in mistaken diagnoses or inappropriate medications/treatments.

We readily understand that physical puberty unfolds at different rates. Some teens grow early and others later, so reassure your child that their time will come. Help them understand that the teen years also bring a neurological puberty, a time of transition when their brains are dramatically remodeled by neuroplasticity. The circuits that have not been used are pruned away to provide more of the brain’s limited resources of oxygen and nutrients to the networks that have been or are being activated (used), which is within their control. The region most actively under construction is the prefrontal cortex, the area where executive functions such as sustained attention, organization, impulse control, planning, and judgment are developing.

The prefrontal cortex is the last major brain system to undergo rapid maturation, with its high responsiveness to activation continuing into the mid-twenties. Just as with physical growth, the timing of this brain maturation varies widely. Two teens of the same age may differ significantly in the development of their attention control systems, not because of intelligence or attitude, but because of developmental timing.

Understanding this difference can reduce your teen’s self-blame and restore hope when they have been given misapplied labels or failed to achieve success in some areas. When they understand that their brain’s control centers for attention will continue to be highly responsive to their efforts to improve, the renewed optimism that hopefully results will help sustain those efforts. Teens benefit from knowing that the prefrontal cortex remains under construction and that variation in timing is normal. This knowledge reduces shame and preserves their willingness to persevere through challenges.

However, teens need more than reassurance alone. They also need practical tools and the chance to practice them. When you help identify strategies and acknowledge their effort, even before there is evidence of full success, you reinforce perseverance. Saying, “I noticed you reset your attention timer and got back on track,” strengthens motivation far more than pointing out what was missed.

Source: snappy goat royalty free

Your Teen's Brain Gets More Information Than It Can Handle

Your teen’s brain receives an enormous amount of sensory input every second, including sounds, sights, internal sensations, thoughts, and emotions. Because it cannot consciously process everything, it relies on an attention filter to decide what deserves priority.

That filter is programmed to attend to novelty, curiosity, and change. Things or information that are surprising, socially relevant, or emotionally stimulating get more intake through the attention system. This is why a phone call while they are doing homework will often pull their attention and focus away from their work and make it take more effort to return to it. This is a reason for them not to keep their phones accessible during homework time.

Active Interventions While Waiting for Maturity

Although full maturation of attention control networks may take years, teens do not have the luxury of waiting as academic demands increase and social pulls intensify.

Those demands on their executive functions, such as focus, make it critical for them to have repeated experiences that strengthen these neural networks. When teens consistently practice strategies that call for focus and self-monitoring, they are literally building and reinforcing the circuits that support attention control.

Source: unsplash royalty free

Motivation is Key

The teen brain has a strong inherent drive for independence and takes real satisfaction in achieving something on its own. Teens want to be in the driver’s seat and not passengers driven by their parents.

That is why the strategies below work best when your teen can see what is in it for them. Knowing that the teen brain is highly responsive to autonomy and purpose, you can raise their motivation to focus by connecting each strategy to something they already want.

When asked what they hoped to gain by strengthening their attention or focus, teens commonly named the following goals, which you can suggest to your child.

  • Finish homework more efficiently
  • Remember what was taught so they would not need to relearn it later
  • Keep track of assignments and materials
  • Catch mistakes before turning in tests
  • Be seen as responsible and capable
  • Have more free time

A Strategy Your Teen Chooses Is One They're More Likely to Use

What follows are strategies to offer your teen, not rules to impose. Introduce one at a time, explain briefly why it works on the brain’s attention filter, and let your teen decide whether to keep it.

  • Suggest writing the most important class notes in a different color, or setting homework notes in a different font. Explain that a change in the visual field gives the attention filter something new to notice, which reboots focus as time passes.
  • Offer fresh air and better light. Their effect fades after a stretch of homework, so opening a window, turning on a brighter lamp, or raising the screen brightness gives the filter a fresh signal. Let your teen notice the difference and decide when to use it.
  • Encourage movement. A few minutes of moving gets the blood flowing and sends a surge of oxygen to the body and brain while flushing away cellular waste. This is more welcome coming as an invitation than as an instruction to get up.
  • Suggest a timer set to sound every fifteen minutes during homework. The signal is not a command to stop. It is a prompt for your teen to ask one question about the last fifteen minutes: was that time used well? If not, they make one adjustment and keep going.
  • Show them the value of not putting an assignment away the moment it is finished. Moving on to the next assignment and returning to the first one later means coming back with a fresher, more alert brain, able to catch errors the first pass missed.
  • Keep a healthy snack within reach so the trip to the kitchen does not become the break. Crunching a carrot or a celery stick is itself a new stimulus that perks up the attention filter.
  • Talk with your teen about where they sit in class. A seat with the strongest sensory access to the sounds, sights, and movements of the instruction gives the attention filter more to work with and avoids extraneous distractions.

As your teen builds stronger attention, you will notice the changes. They begin depending less on your prompts and reminders about assignments and obligations.

As they take increasing charge of their attention, they will persevere longer when a problem confronts them, consider alternative approaches, plan ahead toward a goal, organize their materials, and sustain motivation through setbacks. You will be preparing them for the challenges and opportunities awaiting them now and in their futures.

With your understanding, your encouragement, and strategies they choose for themselves, your teens can make substantial and meaningful changes in their focus and brainpower, even with brains that are still under construction.

item.title: Why Everyone Nodded and Nobody Agreed
item.description:
Leadership

Why Everyone Nodded and Nobody Agreed

Consensus doesn't always mean everyone is on the same page.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Meetings often end in apparent agreement that turns out to be multiple different private pictures.
  • Words alone let listeners quietly fill in gaps with their own assumptions and private interpretations.
  • A shared drawing forces those private pictures into the open so you can avoid the illusion of agreement.
Source: cartoon by author Lisa Rothstein

It happens seemingly every time. The meeting goes well; bullet points are read, discussions are respectful, everyone nods at the end and leaves satisfied they are on the same page.

Then, next time, when you present the work you thought everyone had agreed on, chaos. Everyone appears to have developed amnesia. What you're showing them isn't what they expected. At all.

How is this possible? And why does it happen so often? It happened to me all the time back in my ad agency days. A campaign I was positive had ticked all the boxes got a reaction as if my team had teleported in from Mars. Was it a language problem? I might have believed so when I was working in Paris as a creative director on IBM and Unilever, and we had representatives of up to 17 countries in the room. But the same exact phenomenon took place even on Madison Avenue, when (supposedly) everyone was speaking and understanding English. So what's the problem?

It's Not a Language Problem

The problem wasn't the language. It was the picture. Everyone in that room had been nodding along to the same words, but each of them was quietly building their own private image of what those words meant. And nobody checked whether their images matched. They just assumed they did, because the words did.

At the time, I had built a long and successful career as a copywriter, so while concept was still king in the ad world, words mattered a lot to me. But as a visual thinker, I knew that while the famous cliché said a picture was worth a thousand words, the biggest value of a picture was to short-circuit a thousand misunderstandings.

As a writer and a lover of language, it hurts me to say this, but words on their own can be pretty lousy, or nefarious, communication tools. Depending on the speaker or writer, their skill level and their intention, they can confuse, bloviate, gloss over disagreements, and even intentionally mislead.

How many times have you sat through a presentation given by someone whose language you understand, and who sounded intelligent, but you came away not being able to convey to anyone else what they said? Or you discussed the talk with someone else who was in the same room, but who had a completely different idea of what they heard?

Everyone Co-creates the Story

The study of semiotics tells us that part of this phenomenon stems from personal bias: The reader or listener co-creates the "text." (In this case, a text can be a conversation, a book, a speech, a story, a movie, or even a road sign.) The semiotician Umberto Eco put it well, calling a text "a lazy machine" that depends on the reader to fill in the gaps; we don't just receive meaning, we complete it, using our own experience and assumptions. That's why you experience the same TV show or artwork differently than someone from another cultural background, or even your best friend.

Then there is the strong desire and pressure to come to consensus. No one loves conflict, and everyone wants to feel a meeting was successful, which means something was agreed. Psychologists have a name for what happens next: Joachim Krueger and Russell Clement found that people persistently overestimate how much others agree with them, a bias so stubborn it barely budges even when people are taught about it or shown hard evidence otherwise. With such a bias toward unity and a desire to please, wishful thinking fools us into believing we see things the same way.

Source: sketch by author Lisa Rothstein

And there's a simpler, less flattering reason too: People want to agree with the boss or the client. Not because they've been persuaded, but because they'd rather nod than be the one to challenge authority or the one who just didn't get it.

So, how do we manage this? You probably saw this coming from me, but a great way is to not depend on language alone, where meaning can be twisted, hidden, misconstrued, or simply interpreted differently inside different people’s heads.

Instead, try drawing a picture everyone can see. It can be a very simple diagram, but you’ll be amazed at what it can do.

Don't Just Say It. See It.

When I teach how to do this at innovation conferences, once people get over the idea that they can’t draw, it’s amazing and fascinating how they approach the same problem differently. Instead of forcing agreement or insisting that their way of addressing the issue is the “right” one, participants get genuinely curious and interested in each other’s pictures. The most often-heard phrase in the room is, “Wow! I never would have seen it that way.”

The first time you try this in your own presentation or meeting, you will probably hear at least a few people saying, “Ohhh!” as they finally “get” what you’ve been trying to say. Next, instead of meek or uncertain acquiescence, you’ll have people actively questioning and contributing, as their own mental picture suggested ideas they don’t see reflected yet. Finally, you will have a somewhat messy, but more complete, picture of what everyone, finally, does agree about.

And don’t be too surprised if no one asks for the beautiful slide deck you so carefully prepared, but everyone takes photos of the whiteboard so that they can remember the important work of true consensus you all created together and their role in it.

The best thing about doing this in a meeting is what happens in the next one. Imagine not having to experience any more professional Groundhog Days, where you have to rehash and have the same meeting over and over, where no one is blindsided or confused.

Can you picture it? You should.

item.title: What to Do When Temptation Strikes
item.description:
Self-Control

What to Do When Temptation Strikes

How everyday acts of self-discipline pave a path to self-mastery.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Temptation becomes easier to manage when you name what each side of the conflict is offering.
  • A 10-minute pause can turn an impulse from an instruction into a decision.
  • Self-discipline helps you win the battle, but good systems eliminate the need for a battle in the first place.

We usually know what the right decision is. What we should do.

The problem is that self-discipline is not tested when we are calm and rational.

It is tested when we are hungry, tired, angry, lonely, bored, or stressed—when temptation is more persuasive and long-term goals feel distant.

So, how do we give ourselves a fighting chance in the heat of the moment?

  1. Identify both sides of the conflict: Eating a slice of cake or watching another episode of Netflix is tempting because it offers you some sort of benefit. Acknowledging that benefit allows you to compare it with what you gain by resisting. By seeing clearly how you are being pulled in two directions, you can understand the tension—and choose which direction will serve you better.
  2. Give yourself a 10-minute buffer: Author Daniel Walter explains that one of the most detrimental habits to self-discipline is acting on your impulses without thinking. Sticking to a 10-minute buffer—where you commit to only acting if you still feel like doing so after 10 minutes—gives you a clear window to stop you in your tracks.[1] Practising mindfulness is therefore key to improving self-discipline—if you can become aware of the thoughts and feelings running through your mind, you can notice them without being swayed by them.
  3. Eliminate the need for a battle: While self-discipline will help you win the battle, good systems may eliminate the need for one altogether. For example, stop buying junk food, put your phone in the next room, or block social media apps at certain times of the day.

“Choose rather to punish your appetites than to be punished through them.” —Epictetus[2]

What happens when you keep winning these battles?

Think of self-discipline like a muscle: the more you use it, the stronger it becomes; the less you use it, the more it atrophies. Knowing this allows you to understand which path you are setting yourself on when you face your battle with temptation.

Ironically, the more you win that battle, the less you need self-discipline. The hard things become less hard to overcome, you become more confident in being able to overcome them, and self-discipline becomes part of your identity such that you become someone who does what you say you’re going to do.

Psychiatrist M. Scott Peck went as far as to describe self-discipline as a form of self-care because—by being disciplined—you engage in consistent care and respect towards yourself.[3]

“Self-discipline is self-caring.” —M. Scott Peck

From self-discipline to self-command:

Discipline is resisting the lure of a small reward now for bigger rewards to come. It’s doing what you have to do in the present so you can do what you want to do in the future. It’s giving up the good for the great.

That’s why former Navy SEAL commander Jocko Willink’s bestselling book and life mantra is:

"Discipline equals freedom." [4]

Not freedom from difficulty. Freedom from being controlled by every appetite, emotion, urge, and passing preference that appears. As Epictetus said:

“No man is free who is not master of himself.” [2]

This is where self-discipline leads towards something even more powerful: self-command—the ability to consciously direct your behaviour rather than having it dictated to you by whatever impulse happens to be strongest in the moment.

And downstream of self-command lies self-mastery:

The increasing ability to make your life reflect what you value, rather than merely what you feel like doing.

And that is how we win the inner war: not through one heroic act of willpower, but by repeatedly winning the everyday battles.

item.title: Can Being Creative Actually Make Us Happier?
item.description:
Creativity

Can Being Creative Actually Make Us Happier?

You don’t have to be creative to benefit from creativity.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Creative individuals are not automatically happier than non-creatives.
  • Yet research suggests a positive relationship between creativity and well-being.
  • Participation in creative activities can influence our overall happiness.

Imagine spending some time every day doing something just because it’s enjoyable. It may be crafting a poem, sketching a grandchild, taking wildlife photos, trying a new recipe, arranging your garden, or playing a musical instrument. You’re certainly not an expert in any of these pursuits; you’re doing them simply because they bring you a measure of enjoyment. As such, the simple act of creating something is a valuable part of your life.

Interestingly, a decided body of research is examining a fascinating connection. That is, creative activities aren’t merely an expression of happiness but may actually be one of the pathways that helps us experience more of it. Let’s take a look.

What the Research Says About Creativity and Happiness

A compelling study in 2018 followed 658 young adults for thirteen days, asking them each day about their creative activities, positive and negative emotions, and flourishing. The researchers discovered that subjects experienced greater positive effect and greater flourishing on days following days when they engaged in more creative activities than usual.

Equally important, the researchers did not find the reverse relationship; that is, being happier did not predict greater creativity the following day. The overall conclusion was that creativity may not merely be something we do when we’re feeling good; engaging in creative activities may actually help us feel better.

In a 2021 study, researchers conducted two linked projects. In the first, they examined 256 university students and 291 working adults. They noted a positive relationship between creativity and subjective well-being even after accounting for stress and demographic variables. Subsequently, a follow-up study involving 68 undergraduate students indicated that participants who received a creativity-boosting intervention reported higher subjective well-being than did participants in a control situation. The researchers concluded that increasing creative engagement may, in and of itself, contribute to greater well-being.

Source: RitaE/Pixabay

In another 2021 study researchers synthesized 189 effect sizes from 26 studies involving 8,189 participants. They discovered an overall positive relationship between creativity and well-being (r = .14). Even more significant was that when creativity was measured through actual creative activities and behaviors (rather than laboratory measures of divergent thinking), the relationship with well-being was substantially stronger (r = .22 vs. .06). The overall conclusion was that we don’t necessarily have to be a highly creative person to get the psychological benefits. Doing creative things may matter more than scoring high on a creativity test.

It seems safe to say that science hasn’t proven that creativity always makes us happier. There’s encouraging evidence, but the relationship is complicated and probably bidirectional. Nevertheless, the research evidence seems to support the contention that activities deemed creative can contribute to positive psychological functioning.

Putting Creativity Research Into Practice

There’s evidence to suggest a connection between our engagement in creative activities and our overall psychological happiness. Here are several familiar and enjoyable pastimes that give you an opportunity to influence your overall well-being.

  1. Wonder Walk. Step outside and take a 15-minute walk through your neighborhood, local park or nearby woods. Along the way, look for things that make you say, “I wonder…” Perhaps it’s the leaves on a familiar tree, the movement of an insect, the flowers in a garden, or the sound of a passing bird. Record your questions as soon as you return home – but don’t answer them immediately. Allow your curiosity and imagination to take over.
  2. Happy Memories Collage. Go through your mementos and collect an assortment of photographs, postcards, ticket stubs, children’s drawings, vacation souvenirs and other reminders of happy experiences from your past. Arrange them in a pattern that just feels right for you. You may want to include some key words, a few drawings or a couple of captions. This creative process gives you an opportunity to re-visit happy times and positive experiences while creating something new.
  3. Puzzle Time. Regularly engage with different kinds of puzzles including crossword puzzles, jigsaw puzzles, sudoku, word searches, cryptograms, word jumbles, rebus puzzles, and logic-grid puzzles, among others. Time with a puzzle is a way to exercise your brain and participate in engaging and pleasurable experiences.
  4. Living Room Artist. Walk into your living room and focus your attention on a single object. It may be a vase, a small plant, an unread book, a pillow, the fringe on a rug, or a seldom-used chair. Sketch it, photograph it, describe it in a single sentence, or create a short story about it. This is not an exercise in artistic excellence, but rather an opportunity to express your vision in a variety of ways.
  5. A New Purpose. Pull an item from your trash that you might otherwise throw away. It might be a magazine, a piece of tin foil, a small cardboard box, a yogurt container, or a plastic bottle cap. Challenge yourself to find three creative ways to reuse it. For example, a bottle cap might become a single pill holder, a small hat for a doll, or an ornament for a holiday decoration. This becomes a game of possibilities (“What else could this become?”). You may be surprised at the variety of uses you generate for something you would normally toss.
  6. Six Words. Tap into your memory and identify a particularly happy experience (a recent trip, a day doing nothing, a friend’s comment, or a new restaurant). Express that experience in just six words. For example: “Sunny day. Leafy forest. Quiet walk.” You may want to create a variety of six-word stories—each capturing a small amount of happiness. Interestingly, the word restriction forces your imagination to work in unexpected ways.

Engaging in similar activities such as knitting, gardening, playing music, photography, woodworking, writing, painting, storytelling, and decorating (among others) also provides you with opportunities for creative engagement. In other words, happiness doesn’t necessarily provide the conditions for creativity; creative engagement may itself become a source of happiness.

Final point: Don’t wait until you feel happy to be creative. Engage in a creative activity—and see whether happiness follows.

item.title: The Benefits of an Ageless Workplace
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

The Benefits of an Ageless Workplace

Work is good for all of us.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Employers told Cornell University researchers that new college graduates lack certain skills.
  • Research shows that older workers possess such skills because of their experience.
  • Work provides many benefits, making it good for everyone regardless of age.

Cornell University recently released a report on the future of the American university. Among the many interesting findings in the report was the revelation that employers found new graduates lacking in certain abilities that make a good employee. It wasn’t that the new hires didn’t understand how to do their jobs; in this respect, they were fully qualified. It was rather that the new employees did not possess the “softer” skills that were essential for workers to have in an organization. Specifically, employers said that recent graduates were less than adequately prepared to deal with ambiguity, face criticism, bounce back from failure, and work with colleagues who saw a situation differently.

As the report stated:

"Employers and those who represent their perspectives consistently reported that American graduates, whatever their specialized knowledge, arrive in the workplace without some of the professional capacities the workplace demands. This feedback, corroborated by a National Association of Colleges and Employers survey on employer perceptions of proficiency gaps among recent graduates, centers not on disciplinary knowledge, but on the interpersonal and dispositional skills that allow that disciplinary knowledge to be deployed effectively. These include the ability to handle uncertainty and solve problems that do not have clear answers, a readiness to absorb critical feedback and recover from setbacks, and working in teams that require compromise with others who do not share their perspective or assumptions. While these capacities needed to thrive in complex organizations may seem mundane, employers report encountering them less reliably in new graduates."

The good news is that Cornell has an action plan in place to address this issue as well as other challenges uncovered in its research. In short, there is a need to move higher education from a transactional model, in which the student pays tuition in exchange for knowledge and a credential (degree) to show potential employers, to a transformative model. The latter, according to the report, “locates the value of education not in the credential—an external marker a student can display—but in the graduate’s transformation: the capacities gained that enable contribution in the workplace, community, home, and world.”

Kudos to Cornell for pursuing such a study and taking steps to make its college experience a transformative one. Needless to say, it is in all of our interests to have higher education prepare young adults as best as possible to face the challenges that come with a job and with life in general.

Advantages of Hiring Older Adults

Nowhere in Cornell’s report, however, is it mentioned that there is a very large group of Americans who already possess the skills that employers said new grads didn’t have. While we of course want young adults to find jobs (if only so that they can have places of their own!), there are many older adults in this country who are also seeking employment. In addition to the money, a job provides other important benefits, making work a good thing regardless of one’s age. According to Pivoters.com, which connects people 55+ with employers looking for experienced talent, the United States has “over 100 million people 55 and over, most of whom need to work for financial reasons and want to work for the longevity, health, and social benefits of work.”

To that point, Columbia University’s Mailman School of Public Health has published its own report titled “10 Advantages of Retaining and Hiring Older Workers.” “We heard universally that older workers bring a level of experience, critical thinking and sheer knowledge that cannot be taught,” the report stated, precisely those skills that employers told Cornell they were seeking. As well, the Ohio Department of Aging has published a list of “Truths About Older Workers,” among them:

  • Practical skills: Older adults tend to have superior interpersonal and problem-solving skills and are generally better able to deal with co-workers and customers than their younger counterparts. They also know how to maintain contacts and relationships and seek help when necessary.
  • Patience: Years of experience give older workers the patience to step back and think objectively, rather than react emotionally in stressful situations.
  • Productivity: Workplace wisdom often is the greatest asset of an older worker. Every aspect of job performance improves with experience, especially productivity. Older workers generally know where to invest time and effort to avoid costly mistakes.

Finally, Bain & Company reports that “some 150 million jobs will shift to older workers by 2029,” the reason why the global management consulting firm published “Better With Age: The Rising Importance of Older Workers,” which states:

  • Worker motivations evolve with age, with attributes like interesting work and autonomy rising to the top around age 60.
  • Too few firms recognize the changing needs and priorities of older workers or invest in integrating older workers into their talent system.
  • Leading companies focus on recruiting, retaining, reskilling, and respecting the strengths of this group of workers.
  • Creating roles that benefit both older workers and the company is not just the right thing to do; it’s also a business imperative.

The takeaway from all this excellent research? There are significant gains to be made by creating a workforce composed of Americans of all ages.

item.title: Why Doctors Hide Mistakes
item.description:
Shame

Why Doctors Hide Mistakes

How shame in medical training harms both doctors and patients.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Shame-based medical training teaches doctors to conceal mistakes, implying that only bad doctors make them.
  • Shame after a mistake is linked to higher burnout and depression in doctors.
  • Patients want honesty after an error, and hospitals that disclose and apologize have seen fewer lawsuits.
  • A culture of psychological safety helps doctors own mistakes and keep learning, which improves patient care.

One of my earliest memories of shame in medicine comes from my surgical rotation as a medical student. I woke up at 4 am to be at the hospital by 5 am to round on post-surgical patients. One morning, I forgot to put a patient's identification sticker on the progress note in their paper chart. After my presentation in front of a group of residents and students, the attending called me a "lazy doctor."

My face went hot with shame as I looked down. I had tried so hard, and I didn't know what I could have done better. I thought I had presented well and written a complete progress note. My only mistake was forgetting the sticker.

I never forgot a patient sticker again after that day. I also never forgot the shame of being called a "lazy" doctor.

That's the thing about shame-based teaching: It works—in a way. Shame made sure I never forgot again, but it also taught me that making a mistake meant I was a "bad" doctor.

I wasn't alone. Students traded stories all the time, including one about a progress note torn up in front of the group because it was "bad." Fear and shame pushed us to work harder, not because we wanted to be good doctors, but because we didn't want to be bad ones. The takeaway was that good doctors don't make mistakes; only bad doctors do.

This conditioning repeated itself for years, across medical school, hospitals, and rotations. So it's no wonder doctors hide their errors.

Unfortunately, this creates a deeper problem. If a good doctor is someone who never makes mistakes, then admitting one threatens not just your competence but your sense of who you are. A mistake doesn't just make you a bad doctor—it makes you a bad person.

Guilt vs. Shame

It’s important to note the distinction between guilt and shame. Guilt says, "I did something bad, but I'm still a good person." Shame says, "I did something bad because I am bad."

This subtle difference changes behavior. Research by psychologist June Tangney found that guilt tends to motivate people to apologize, make amends, and try to do better. Shame, on the other hand, pushes people to hide, deny, or deflect blame, because a mistake feels like proof that they are a bad person. In medicine, shame and self-judgment after mistakes are linked with increased burnout, depression, and poorer well-being in physicians.

Looking back, I can see that when my attending called me a "lazy doctor," he wasn't correcting a missing sticker. He was judging who I was. That's how shame-based teaching works, and it's why it produces physicians who learn to conceal mistakes rather than confront them.

Is There a Better Way to Handle Medical Mistakes?

Concealment might protect a doctor's ego, but it doesn't protect patients. Doctors are humans, and humans make errors. Sooner or later, every doctor will make a mistake. The real question is what the doctor does afterward.

Because mistakes in medicine can be life-threatening, there is very little room for them. A mistake signals incompetence, and near-misses and errors get swept under the rug. Yet that silence is exactly what keeps errors from being fixed. In her research, Harvard professor Amy Edmondson found that better-functioning teams appeared to report more errors, not fewer. They weren't making more mistakes. They just felt safe enough to talk about them, which is what allowed them to improve.

Increased transparency benefits patients and doctors alike. Many doctors worry that admitting a mistake will lead to a lawsuit or to them being viewed as a “bad” doctor. However, studies have found that patients want to be told when an error has occurred, with an honest explanation and an apology. When the University of Michigan Health System adopted a program of disclosing errors, apologizing, and offering fair compensation, researchers reported that lawsuits and liability costs went down. Similarly, after a Tennessee hospital adopted a communication-and-resolution program, claims filed in court decreased by 42 percent. This shows that patients value honesty and integrity in their physicians, even when something goes wrong.

The good news is that medical education is shifting. Driven in part by feedback from trainees, training programs are shifting away from traditional shame-based teaching and toward environments that foster psychological safety, where learners can say "I don't know" or "I made a mistake" without being humiliated. Faculty development now places greater emphasis on nonviolent communication and feedback that addresses behavior and milestones rather than passing judgment on a person's character. "This chart needs a patient label and here's why it matters for safety" teaches the same lesson as "lazy doctor," without the lasting shame.

Good Doctors Learn From Mistakes

I believe a doctor who can't admit a mistake is more dangerous to you as a patient than a doctor who can.

Of course, everyone wants a knowledgeable doctor who knows what they're doing. But you also want one with the humility to say, "I got that wrong, and here's what I'm changing," and the curiosity to keep learning as medicine evolves.

As a patient, you can look for a doctor who explains their reasoning, welcomes your questions, and is comfortable saying, "I'm not sure. Let me look into that." Rather than signs of incompetence, they’re signs of an honest doctor you can trust.

I still think about that morning on my surgical rotation. The attending taught me to pay attention to details and never forget a sticker. But the shame he used to teach that lesson stayed with me. It took me years to unlearn that my worth as a person depended on my performance as a doctor. Today, I know those two things are separate. A mistake is something I did, not who I am, and certainly not a judgment of my character.

Shame thrives in silence, and it loses its power when we name it. So when I make a mistake now, I try to name it, own it, and learn from it, without letting shame tell me I'm a bad doctor. I try to offer the students and residents I teach that same grace, not because standards don't matter, but because they do. Every time we respond to a mistake with curiosity instead of shame, we help build a culture where doctors can admit errors, learn from them, and keep patients safer. A doctor who isn't ruled by shame is a doctor who's a life-long learner, and that's the doctor every patient deserves.

item.title: Should Atheists Pray?
item.description:
Religion

Should Atheists Pray?

How arguments for prayer appear incoherent.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • We can get psychological benefits from many activities, but that doesn’t mean we should engage in them.
  • Praying just in case God exists mirrors Pascal's wager, but faces the "Many Gods" objection.
  • Rationality in prayer hinges on acknowledging countless equally probable deities, not just one.

Recently, a fellow philosopher offered an interesting and provocative philosophical argument that even atheists should pray. As I'll try to show here, I don't think that argument works.

Suppose that you think there is a 5% chance that you have a powerful benefactor who can move heaven and Earth on your behalf. You can send out letters which he will read if he exists. It seems worth doing this sometimes. Sure, probably nobody is listening, but if someone is, the action has very great value.

Likewise, suppose you are an atheist. You think God probably doesn’t exist. Nonetheless, being open-minded, you think there’s some chance God exists—maybe 5%, maybe 1%. On similar grounds, it seems to make sense to pray. If there is a God, this action could have very great value. If there isn’t a God, then the action is at worst a waste of a minute every day—with the upside of various psychological benefits.

Let’s get psychological benefits out of the way first. No atheist has to deny those. We can derive psychological benefits from all kinds of activities, but that doesn’t mean we should engage in them. The question is rather whether prayer offers psychological benefits beyond those of other activities and whether those alleged benefits would continue to exist even if you don’t believe prayer works. He goes on to argue:

My sense is that the psychological literature is pretty clear that wishing people well improves your welfare and makes you more empathetic. Thinking hard about the importance of another person’s welfare is a good idea, even if there is no God.

But that reference goes to meditation. Not prayer. Even Sam Harris, as an anti-theist, recommends meditation. So these two distinct activities, among the many other activities one can engage in, such as donating to the poor or helping in a soup kitchen, should not be used as support for prayer over other such activities. Indeed, directly helping people not only makes one more empathetic; it also helps them.

So let us focus on the expected causal consequences via a god’s interventions in the world.

if there is a God, your actions might have various desirable effects. God, on standard views, hears our prayers, and sometimes his plans are different because of our prayers than they would have otherwise been. Even short of a direct miracle, God might, in his providence, order things towards bringing about the results of our prayers. At the very least, I don’t think this kind of thing is extremely unlikely if God exists, so it’s still a pretty good bet.

On the face of it, Adelstein’s argument may seem compelling. But isn’t this just a version of Pascal’s wager according to which it seems that belief in God always carries a higher expected value?

Not quite, since most people think that it is irrational to believe something on grounds of the benefits that it would bring. What matters is the evidence. But Adelstein isn’t asking atheists to believe in God. He only argues that it would be rational to engage in the action of prayer.

However, there is another objection to Pascal’s wager that does apply to Adelstein’s argument: The Many Gods Objection. Given the hundreds, nay, thousands of religions, the table above would be radically altered since it is no longer a choice between theism and atheism, but between atheism and thousands of alternative gods one may believe in, many of which may not look kindly upon prayer for "false gods."

The same goes for prayer. Adelstein writes:

I don’t think it makes sense for this to be a lengthy and protracted ordeal if you’re an atheist. But it seems like every day for maybe a minute, you should pray to God so that you can know, love, and serve him, if he really exists.

But while it may not seem costly to pray for a minute or so each day, things suddenly become quite costly once we allow for the possibility that several gods are equally likely. Really, Adelstein’s logic recommends that we become like Beni Gabor, the superstitious and greed-driven character from one of my favourite movies, 1999’s The Mummy. Beni, ever the opportunist, carries several religious symbols with him and learns the languages of different religions to cover his bases. As Adelstein puts it, this should be seen as a good bet. Indeed, in the movie, that briefly works out for him when he ends up praying to several gods.

Theists may believe that there is a good chance for the existence of a god. They may find the many arguments proposed by religious folks to rationalize their faiths convincing. After all, the scientific worldview can admittedly seem depressing. No afterlife. No reward for good behaviour. No punishment for the wicked. But almost none of these arguments favour one religion over another. No theist should be dogmatic about their particular religious denomination. As Adelstein writes:

This case gets weaker if you are extremely confident that there’s no God. But probably you shouldn’t be that confident. A lot of smart people disagree with you. In general, when smart people have thought hard about a question and disagree with you in droves, you shouldn’t be ridiculously confident that you’re right and they’re wrong. If we all followed this advice, on average, we’d have much more accurate beliefs.

Much like Adelstein wants atheists to at least allow for a small probability that theism is true, a good Bayesian should also allow for the possibility that hundreds of alternative religions could be correct. If you think you should pray, then you should really pray to all of these religions. A minute a day suddenly turns into several hours. If theists were consistent, this is what they should do, but it’s so evidently self-defeating that this consequence should really call into question the very idea of prayer at all.

item.title: The Hidden Cost of Dehumanising Workplace Language
item.description:
Cognition

The Hidden Cost of Dehumanising Workplace Language

The metaphors we use at work shape how we see others — and ourselves.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Workplace metaphors shape how we see people, value and work.
  • Calling people "resources," "capital" or "dead wood" can distance us from the human consequences of decisions.
  • We internalise workplace language, learning to judge ourselves by productivity, performance and value.
Human Resources
Source: Steve A. Johnson / Unsplash

One of the many things that makes me sad about the modern workplace: we seem to have collectively accepted using dehumanising language when we talk about humans in organisational structure.

We call ourselves human resources or human capital. We are assets to be sweated. We make up headcount. We are placed in talent pools, moved through pipelines; we get deployed, utilised, optimised, upskilled and restructured. When we cease to be useful, we become dead weight and are severed, fired or made redundant while organisations undertake some judicious rightsizing.

And now everyone talks about human skills. It is not quite in the same category of cannon fodder, and I understand what the phrase is trying to do. In the age of the AI work revolution, where we no longer have an exclusively human workforce, it seeks to identify the capacities that remain distinctively ours. But there is something peculiar about having to put human in front of skills at all. Whose skills did we think they were? And why define ourselves as a species in terms of the relative usefulness of our skill sets in business environments, and, more specifically, the usefulness of our skill sets measured against a technology we ourselves have created?

The kind of dehumanising workplace language to which human skills belong, however, is not in itself a new phenomenon. It has a much longer history. This history is very telling about the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves at work.

Work Metaphors We Live By

Our language, including the language of work, is riddled with metaphor. Most are so familiar that we no longer even recognise them as figurative language. But metaphors matter. The danger begins when we forget that the metaphor is a metaphor, and start mistaking the world it creates for reality itself. Metaphors are not merely decorative linguistic flourishes. They are culturally sanctioned ways of seeing and thinking, and they substantially shape how we experience the world. Every metaphor invites a specific connection between two different domains, and it thus illuminates certain aspects of reality while making others disappear. The metaphors we use tell their own story about how we see ourselves, other people, and the broader context in which we relate to one another.

Think of an organisation as a machine and people become cogs: efficiency and productivity must be maximised at all costs, friction must be eliminated, glitches fixed. Think of it as a body and there is fat to trim, diseased tissue to remove, and organisational health to restore. A garden gives us dead wood, weeds, cultivation, and growth. Business as warfare brings targets, campaigns, hostile takeovers, and front lines. We may be OK about inflicting collateral damage and casualties as normalised battle costs.

Researchers studying the language of work have long noted these patterns. Metaphors do much more than simply describe organisational life: they make certain actions appear natural, necessary, and benign. Horticultural metaphors turn dismissals into healthy pruning; medical metaphors make redundancies therapeutic interventions; military metaphors turn human costs into strategic necessities; mechanistic metaphors make people interchangeable.

All of these metaphors are euphemisms that create distance by dehumanising human actors. Nobody loses the mortgage-paying job they have held for 15 years. Nobody has to go home and tell their partner that their income has vanished. Nobody experiences shame, fear, anger, or grief. Metaphor becomes a shield against empathy.

Alienated from Ourselves

These metaphors reveal the stories beneath the official stories. Organisations are saturated with narratives about what people are, what work is for, what counts as value, and what can legitimately be sacrificed in its pursuit. Some stories appear explicitly in strategies and values statements. Others hide in plain sight in the language we use. I call the capacity to notice and work consciously with these narratives Story Intelligence.

The really curious thing is that the dehumanising workplace language is not simply imposed upon workers by a sinister managerial class. We all use it. We have long internalised these terms. What is worse, they have a palpable psychological effect on us and structure how we experience ourselves and others in the workplace, and even how we may think of our value as human beings.

We worry about our productivity and our output. We talk about optimising our performance, maximising our potential, increasing our efficiency and upgrading our skill sets. We fear becoming obsolete and redundant, surplus to requirement. We have become extraordinarily fluent in speaking about ourselves in business language terms, assessing our value from an economic utility point of view.

And there is a cost to that. Research on organisational dehumanisation links being treated primarily as an instrument for organisational ends with lower wellbeing, diminished dignity, loss of engagement, and greater intentions to leave.

But I think there is another, subtler consequence. We begin to look at ourselves through the same instrumental lens. Instead of asking How am I? we ask: How am I performing? Instead of What do I need? we ask: How can I become more productive? Instead of What matters to me? we wonder: What value am I adding? Instead of What kind of life do I want? we think: How can I optimise myself and remain competitive?

This is alienation in a particularly intimate form: we not only learn to experience ourselves as the thing being managed, but we become both manager and resource.

Change the Metaphor, Change the Story

Which brings us back to human skills. As machines perform more tasks once regarded as distinctly human, we have begun to compile lists of our remaining competitive advantages: empathy, creativity, curiosity, judgement, emotional intelligence, story intelligence, moral and ethical reasoning, imagination, and the capacity to relate and form bonds tend to feature.

But notice what we are doing here. Even while trying to define and defend our humanity, we translate it into the language of economic utility. Empathy becomes valuable because AI cannot do it as well. Creativity becomes a competitive differentiator. Curiosity becomes a future-ready capability. Here is the sad irony: Essentially, we defend our humanity by writing a business case for it.

Story leadership begins with attention. What metaphors dominate your thinking and your organisation? Machine, family, ecosystem, team, army, body, marketplace? What do they make visible – and what do they make impossible to see? Most importantly, what do these metaphors do to your people?

Language does not merely describe organisational reality. Repeated often enough, it helps create it. If we want more human workplaces, adding human to our skills, resources, or capital will not be enough. We need to examine the story underneath.

And perhaps we can begin with the strange fact that we ever agreed to call ourselves human resources in the first place.

item.title: How to Use Our Screening Playbook to Enhance Dating Success
item.description:
Mating

How to Use Our Screening Playbook to Enhance Dating Success

Don’t date the résumé—date the trajectory.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Choose for future potential not just present fit: A great partner is someone willing and able to keep growing.
  • Look for real personal growth, not just promotions: Self-awareness and change matter more than a shiny résumé.
  • Pay attention to whether they can change their minds: Relationships need curiosity, humility, and flexibility.

Dating apps encourage us to judge people as they are right now. We look at photos, education, profession, interests, sense of humor, and perhaps whether they own an alarming number of cats.

In other words: Is this person a good fit for me?

But when we hire people at my company, particularly people whose potential may have been overlooked by other employers, we try to ask a different question:

Who could this person become?

That might be a useful question in dating, too.

Psychologists distinguish between “destiny beliefs”—the idea that relationships either work or they don't—and “growth beliefs,” the belief that good relationships can be built and improved. Research suggests that people with stronger growth beliefs may maintain relationship satisfaction better over time.

So, once you've swiped right and moved beyond “What do you do?” and “Where do you live?” consider listening for trajectory rather than perfection.

1. Has this person actually grown?

In a job interview, we might ask:

“What's something you weren't very good at five years ago that you've become better at?”

Please don't ask exactly that on a first date. You may never get a second.

Instead, when someone mentions their earlier years, an old job, or a past relationship, you might naturally say:

“Do you think you've changed much since then?”

Or:

“What do you think you've gotten better at as you've gotten older?”

You're listening for evidence that the person learns and changes—not merely accumulates birthdays.

2. Have they developed, not just advanced?

Someone can become richer, more senior, and more successful while remaining precisely the same person.

At work, I might ask:

“What's something you've changed about yourself because someone gave you honest feedback?”

On a date, when discussing an appropriate topic, like people who are judgmental or who are too forthcoming with feedback, you could simply ask:

“Has anyone ever told you something about yourself that annoyed you at first—but you eventually realized they were right?”

That answer can reveal considerably more than their job title.

3. Do they repair relationships—or simply replace people?

At work:

“Tell me about a difficult relationship with a colleague that you managed to improve.”

On a date, again, when the topic is appropriate (don't ask out of the blue…):

“Have you ever really fallen out with a friend or family member and then managed to become close again?”

Then listen to how they talk about people generally. If every former partner was a narcissist, every boss an idiot, every friend selfish, and every neighbor impossible, statistically speaking, there may eventually be one more unreasonable person in their life:

You.

4. Can they tolerate being wrong?

At work:

“Tell me about a time somebody changed your mind about something important.”

On a date: share an incident in which you had an opinion about something, but after a while you realized or were convinced by someone that you were wrong. Then you can ask:

“Have you ever been completely convinced about something and then done a total U-turn?”

Or simply:

“Are you good at admitting you're wrong?”

If they answer, “Yes, although it rarely happens,” you have learned something useful.

None of this means that you should be turning dinner into an assessment center; dating is supposed to be enjoyable. So, the right time to ask any of these questions is when they flow from the topic of conversation and don't hinder it.

When looking for a serious partner, perhaps we put too much emphasis on their current fit. The person who looks perfect today may not necessarily be the best partner 10 years from now. A better emphasis may be not just “How well do we fit?” but “Are we both the kind of people who can keep growing together?”

item.title: Improving Group Decision-Making
item.description:
Decision-Making

Improving Group Decision-Making

When groupthink and the Abilene paradox are problems.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Groupthink is the failure to manage disagreement.
  • The Abilene paradox is the failure to manage agreement.
  • Understanding and dealing with groupthink and the Abilene paradox can improve group decision-making.
Source: RosZie / Pixabay

At work, in our communities, and among friends and family, we often make decisions in groups. From major business decisions to what to do on a Saturday night, in groups, we make decisions big and small. What is the quality of those decisions? Sometimes we need to make the best decision possible. Other times, we just need a decision that works. In group decisions, there are two concepts that can affect the quality of those decisions. One is groupthink, a word often used but not necessarily understood. The other, the Abilene paradox, is lesser known.

In healthy group decision-making, two social psychological processes are ongoing. First, the group seeks to make a decision, find a solution, resolve some issue, make a determination, find an answer. This is the process of integration—that is, bringing together diverse ideas and information to make a good decision. That good decision usually involves critical discussion of alternatives, looking at pros and cons of various options. This is the process of differentiation. If integration and/or differentiation break down in a group discussion, the odds are the decision will not be as good as it might have been.

Groupthink

Groupthink is the inability to manage disagreement. William H. Whyte coined this term in a 1952 Fortune magazine article. Later, in 1971, in a Psychology Today article and then a 1972 book, Irving Janis elaborated on this concept, creating a diagnostic framework. Among the symptoms of groupthink he identified were applying pressure on dissenters, people not sharing their ideas (self-censorship), and “a shared illusion of unanimity.” Consider this tale:

A decision is needed. The boss convenes a meeting of the six supervisors.

The boss says, “We have a problem. To save money, we need to start laying off people.”

One supervisor follows, “Seems like that’s what we need to do. I agree, Taylor.”

Someone else: “Yeah, Taylor. I think that is the way to go.”

Another: “Tough decision, but we have to do what we have to do.”

The other supervisors say nothing. One supervisor thinks there are lots of ways to save money without laying off employees. Another sees this as a bad decision. Good employees are just hard to find. A third supervisor thinks they ought to brainstorm other solutions.

“Well, it looks like we are in agreement. We’ll start layoffs in two weeks.”

The boss didn’t try to hear from three of the supervisors. She could have solicited their input. Were layoffs the best solution? The only solution? There was no differentiation, no discussion of pros and cons. The boss failed to get everyone’s input. Three of the supervisors failed to express their views. They may have thought the decision was already made or speaking up might cost them some social capital.

So what to do? As a leader, be open to other ideas and solicit them. Another approach is to appoint someone or several people to express any reservations or comment critically about the possible solutions presented. This is called appointing a “devil’s advocate” or “disrupters.”

The Abilene Paradox

The Abilene paradox is the inability to manage agreement. Jerry Harvey introduced this concept in 1974 in an article in Organizational Dynamics. He told a story about a family with visiting in-laws. They decided to take a trip, hot and dusty, to Abilene to eat a meal when, in fact, that is not what any of them actually wanted to do. Although they did not know it, they all were in agreement about just staying at home. No one had expressed their true opinion.

Harry and four of his friends enjoyed doing things together. He was extroverted and usually the one who suggested activities. He was satisfied with golfing occasionally and poker nights, but he thought his buddies might like to do something different.

One weekend when they were hanging out, Harry said, “I’ve been thinking. How would you guys like for us to form a bowling team and join a league? Might be fun.” Harry actually didn’t enjoy bowling much but thought his friends might, so he just tossed out the idea.

Steve replied, “Why not, Harry. I haven’t tried bowling, but I could learn.” Truthfully, Steve had no interest in a bowling team. One by one, all supported the idea and concealed how they really felt about a bowling team. No one was really interested, but since Harry proposed it, they didn’t want to let him down. They ended up joining a league but quit at their first opportunity.

They had just done something that no one, not even Harry, really wanted to do, something about which they were in total agreement. They ended up doing it because nobody would say what they really thought. There was no differentiation.

For groups to come to the best decisions, everyone needs to be involved, stating opinions and discussing pros and cons. Understanding the problems inherent in groupthink and the Abilene paradox can improve group decision-making and help groups of which we are part make better decisions.
